name: Wayfinch AI
tagline: Find the right AI tool. Then learn the route.
positioning: Wayfinch AI is the field guide for non-technical people who want to pick one AI tool for a real task and learn it through short, numbered tutorial trails instead of hype-driven lists.
audience: Curious beginners, freelancers, teachers and small-team operators who feel overwhelmed by the number of AI tools and want plain-language guidance tied to everyday tasks.
strategy: Organise discovery by task, not by hype: a filterable directory where every tool listing links to a step-by-step trail. Build trust with a transparent review method and privacy-first questions, then grow community through free live 'Tool Walk' sessions and a weekly newsletter.

contrastPairs.use: text on yellow panels and highlights
text on orange chips, step numbers and CTA
small orange labels on paper (darkened orange)

artDirection: Every creative reads like a page from a friendly trail guide: warm paper background, Night Map ink, and one bold Compass Blue or Night Map block for weight. A dotted Finch Orange route should always lead the eye from headline to content to CTA, with numbered stops when steps are involved. Keep headlines short and set in Archivo Black, supporting copy in Archivo, and show the finch somewhere as the guide. Tool names are always fictional and framed as examples, never endorsements.

name: Fixturehaus
tagline: Every kickoff. Under the lights.
positioning: Fixturehaus is the matchday football publication that turns fixture lists, previews and scorecards into bold, scannable kit-graphic stories for fans who plan their weekend around kickoff.
audience: Matchday fans aged 18-40 who follow several clubs, check fixtures on their phone between Friday and Monday, and want fast, confident previews rather than long-form punditry.
strategy: Own the 72 hours before kickoff with a fixture board, data-led previews and a free predictor league that builds a weekly ritual. Every format leads with the matchup (VS split, scoreboard, table) so a post reads in under three seconds in the feed. Community features reward opinions and bragging rights, never betting.

contrastPairs.use: large display type and graphics only (not body text)

artDirection: Every creative leads with the matchup: a VS split, a fixture board or a table, set in towering Bebas Neue with Rubik doing the explaining. Night-pitch green is the stage, floodlight glows light it from the top corners, and faint pitch markings anchor the grid. Yellow is reserved for kickoff times and CTAs, red for the away side and SAMPLE labels, green for the home side and data. All clubs, players and numbers are fictional and every story is labelled as a sample.

name: Halfline Journal
tagline: The rest of the story, told slowly.
positioning: Halfline Journal is a multi-sport longform publication that treats athletes, grounds and seasons with the patience of documentary photojournalism, publishing fewer stories that go much further.
audience: Thoughtful sports readers aged 25-55 who follow several sports, read weekend features, listen to documentary podcasts and want the human story behind results rather than another hot take.
strategy: Own the slow lane of sports media: one flagship longform feature a week, serialised in numbered chapters, with a strong monochrome visual identity that stands out in colour-saturated sports feeds. Social works as a trailer for the chapters (carousel covers, contact sheets, reporting notes) and drives sign-ups to the Sunday Long Read newsletter. All stories in this concept are clearly labelled SAMPLE STORY and feature fictional athletes, teams and places.

contrastPairs.use: body text and headlines on newsprint
kickers, links and SAMPLE labels on newsprint
button and CTA text on red
captions and metadata on darkroom sections
red kicker text on darkroom sections (tint of Rule Red)

artDirection: Every creative should feel like a page lifted from a serious weekend broadsheet: newsprint or darkroom black backgrounds, one grainy monochrome plate, and red used sparingly as a rule, a circle or a single call to action. Headlines are set big in DM Serif Display with an italic second line, supported by small tracked Libre Franklin kickers and captions. Chapter numerals, plate captions and SAMPLE STORY labels appear on every piece so the series logic is legible at a glance. Avoid colour photography, gradients in hue, emoji and stadium-hype language.

name: The Plainwire
tagline: News, explained plainly.
positioning: The Plainwire turns complicated local and current-affairs stories into clear, neutral, numbered explainers that separate what is known from what is not yet known.
audience: Busy, curious adults (25–60) who want to understand civic, transport, energy and community news without spin, jargon or a doom-scroll.
strategy: Lead with wire-service rigor and a repeatable explainer format: numbered cards, timeline strips and 'What we know' boxes that readers learn to trust at a glance. Grow habit through The Daily Five newsletter and community formats like Ask the Explainer, keeping every story sourced, neutral and dated.

contrastPairs.use: body text in What we know boxes and cards
SAMPLE STORY labels and alert kickers

artDirection: Every creative reads like a calm front page: a hairline ink rule under the logo, a blue uppercase kicker, then a Newsreader headline with one italic blue phrase. Structure carries the design, so use numbered cards, What we know boxes, timeline strips and pinned maps instead of decoration. Red is reserved for SAMPLE labels, the wire's end node and 'not yet known' signals; never for alarmism. Keep backgrounds white or Desk Grey, with one full-bleed Wire Blue panel at most per piece.

name: Paintcourt
tagline: Basketball culture, printed loud.
positioning: Paintcourt is a riso-printed, zine-spirited basketball culture publication that covers the game from the blacktop up: players, sneakers, courts and style, told with the energy of a 90s photocopied fanzine.
audience: Culture-first hoops fans aged 16 to 35 who care as much about the fit, the sneakers and the neighbourhood court as the box score; streetwear collectors, rec-league players and designers.
strategy: Lead with a collectible weekly 'issue' format so every post feels like a page torn from a zine, not a scoreboard update. Pair editorial features with community moments (court repaints, sneaker anatomy, data zines) so the brand earns a place both online and on the court. Every story is clearly labelled as a fictional sample story for this concept brand.

contrastPairs.use: body text on ink sections and story-format creatives
body text on purple color blocks
buttons, highlight bars and text on orange blocks

artDirection: Every creative should feel like a page from a photocopied 90s fanzine: one bold color block, one oversized Rubik Mono One headline with an orange highlight bar, and a collage of stickers, tape and court-key linework. Use halftone dots and a light grain overlay for risograph texture; never use photography or real players, teams, leagues or sneaker brands. Rotate supporting labels 2 to 12 degrees, keep headlines straight and legible, and always label editorial content as a fictional SAMPLE STORY.

name: Diodeline
tagline: Tech news, traced to the source.
positioning: Diodeline is the tech newsroom that turns launch-day noise into dated briefings, versioned explainers and spec cards that print the fine print, so readers know what a claim actually depends on.
audience: Curious, busy gadget owners and early-career tech professionals (24-45) who want to decide whether to update, upgrade or wait without wading through hype.
strategy: Own clarity over speed: every story is dated, every explainer is versioned, and every spec claim carries its condition. A running changelog and a weekday email build a habit, while social turns the method itself (spec cards, launch anatomy, Ask the Desk) into save-worthy, shareable formats.

contrastPairs.use: body text and headlines on light
labels on green chips and buttons

artDirection: Compose every piece like a circuit board: a dark substrate or a light cleanroom grid, with one signal-green trace carrying the eye from the headline to the evidence. Headlines are heavy Red Hat Display set tight, with violet reserved for the key word; all metadata (dates, versions, SAMPLE labels) lives in Red Hat Mono chips. Each asset shows the method, not hype: spec claims always appear with their condition, and timelines read like changelogs. Keep one diode mark visible, generous 64px+ margins and no more than one accent colour per focal point.
